sat-practice-test.alt: Timeline of the Digital SAT showing two 32-minute Reading and Writing modules, a break, and two 35-minute Math modules drawn to scale.
sat-practice-test.figAlt: Two rows of question dots: about 14 of 27 Reading and Writing questions done with 16 minutes left, and about 11 of 22 Math questions done with 17 to 18 minutes left.
sat-practice-test.caption: Rough pacing checkpoints for one module. Treat them as a guide, not a rule.

digital-sat-format.alt: Diagram of the adaptive Digital SAT: a first module of mixed difficulty leads to either an easier or a harder second module in each section.
digital-sat-format.figAlt: Two columns listing the four Reading and Writing domains and the four Math domains of the Digital SAT.
digital-sat-format.caption: The four domains of each section, as College Board describes them.

sat-math-practice-questions.alt: Four boxes naming the SAT Math domains: Algebra, Advanced Math, Problem-Solving and Data Analysis, and Geometry and Trigonometry, each with a sample expression.
sat-math-practice-questions.figAlt: Four-step loop for SAT Math questions: read what is asked, translate to an equation, solve, then check the answer against the question.
sat-math-practice-questions.caption: The same four steps apply to every SAT Math domain.

sat-grammar-rules.alt: Cheat sheet showing three correct ways to join two independent clauses: comma plus conjunction, semicolon, and colon, and the comma splice error to avoid.
sat-grammar-rules.figAlt: Sentence 'The box of old photographs is in the attic' with the phrase 'of old photographs' crossed out and an arrow linking the subject 'box' to the verb 'is'.
sat-grammar-rules.caption: Find the true subject by crossing out the phrase between it and the verb.

sat-reading-practice-questions.alt: Two columns grouping SAT Reading question types: Information and Ideas (central ideas, evidence, inferences) and Craft and Structure (words in context, structure and purpose, cross-text connections).
sat-reading-practice-questions.figAlt: Four-step method for SAT reading questions: read the question first, find the key line in the passage, predict an answer in your own words, then eliminate choices that do not match.
sat-reading-practice-questions.caption: A short routine for any reading question.

sat-mock-test-review.alt: Example error log with columns for question, skill, why it was missed, and the fix, with two sample rows about percentages and subject-verb agreement.
sat-mock-test-review.figAlt: Five labeled boxes for the reasons students miss SAT questions: content gap, trap answer, misreading, careless slip, and time pressure, each with its fix.
sat-mock-test-review.caption: Naming the reason tells you what to practice next.

sat-study-plan.alt: Six-week SAT study timeline: week 1 baseline practice test, weeks 2 and 3 fix weaknesses, week 4 second practice test, week 5 mixed timed practice, week 6 final test and test-day readiness.
sat-study-plan.figAlt: Stacked bar of a 50-minute SAT study session: 10 minutes on the rule, 30 minutes of practice on one skill, and 10 minutes on the error log.
sat-study-plan.caption: The study-session pattern used in weeks 2 and 3.

sat-percentage-problems.alt: Bar chart: a quantity starts at 100, increases 20 percent to 120, then decreases 20 percent to 96, which is 4 percent lower than the start.
sat-percentage-problems.figAlt: Four cards showing multipliers: 15 percent increase is times 1.15, 25 percent decrease is times 0.75, 5 percent growth for 3 years is 1.05 cubed, and a reverse percent divides by the multiplier.
sat-percentage-problems.caption: Multipliers make every percent question a one-line calculation.

sat-circle-questions.alt: Circle of radius 8 with a 120 degree sector shaded, labeled with arc length 16π/3 and sector area 64π/3, each one third of the circumference and area.
sat-circle-questions.figAlt: Coordinate grid with a circle centered at (3, −2) with radius 5, showing that the center signs are opposite those in the equation.
sat-circle-questions.caption: In (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r², the center is (h, k) and the radius is the square root of the right side.

sat-linear-equations-and-functions.alt: Graph of the line f(x) = 2x + 10 through (−5, 0) and (−4, 2) with a slope triangle showing a run of 1 and a rise of 2.
sat-linear-equations-and-functions.figAlt: Graph of a phone plan cost C = 0.15m + 20 against minutes used, showing the 20 dollar intercept as the fixed monthly fee and the slope 0.15 as the cost per minute.
sat-linear-equations-and-functions.caption: In a word problem, the intercept is the starting value and the slope is the rate of change.

sat-quadratic-equations.alt: Parabola f(x) = (x − 3)² − 4 with its vertex at (3, −4) and x-intercepts at (1, 0) and (5, 0).
sat-quadratic-equations.figAlt: Three small parabolas: one crossing the x-axis twice when the discriminant is positive, one touching it once when zero, and one never reaching it when negative.
sat-quadratic-equations.caption: Positive, zero, or negative discriminant: two, one, or no real solutions.

sat-systems-of-equations.alt: Two lines for adult and child ticket counts crossing at (20, 30), the solution to a + c = 50 and 12a + 8c = 480.
sat-systems-of-equations.figAlt: Three panels of two lines: different slopes cross once (one solution), same slope different intercepts are parallel (no solution), and identical lines overlap (infinitely many solutions).
sat-systems-of-equations.caption: The three possible outcomes for a system of two linear equations.

sat-probability-two-way-tables.alt: Two-way table of juniors and seniors by whether they have a job, with the juniors row highlighted to show the probability 18 out of 60.
sat-probability-two-way-tables.figAlt: Three copies of a two-way table highlighting a row total, a column total, and the grand total as the denominator for different probability questions.
sat-probability-two-way-tables.caption: The denominator is the group the question restricts you to.

sat-transitions-questions.alt: Chart of transition word families: contrast, cause and effect, addition, example, and sequence, each with sample words.
sat-transitions-questions.figAlt: Flow showing two sentences about early telescopes joined by a blank; the second sentence limits the first, so the relationship is contrast and the answer is a contrast word.
sat-transitions-questions.caption: Read both sentences, name how they relate, and only then look at the choices.

sat-vocabulary-words-in-context.alt: Sample SAT words-in-context question with a blank and four choices, where 'reproducible' is checked because other labs repeated the experiment.
sat-vocabulary-words-in-context.figAlt: The word 'dense' used in two sentences: a dense forest means thick, while a dense argument means hard to follow, each with its context clue highlighted.
sat-vocabulary-words-in-context.caption: Many SAT vocabulary words have several meanings. The clues around the blank pick one.

mastering-sat-math-practice-linear-inequ.alt: Number line showing the solution x < −2 to the inequality 3 − 2x > 7, with an open circle at −2 and shading to the left, and the steps showing the sign flip.
mastering-sat-math-practice-linear-inequ.figAlt: Four number lines showing x less than 1 (open circle, shade left), x less than or equal to 1 (closed circle, shade left), x greater than 1 (open circle, shade right), and x greater than or equal to 1 (closed circle, shade right).
mastering-sat-math-practice-linear-inequ.caption: Strict inequalities use an open circle; inequalities that include equality use a closed circle.

sat-math-prep-exponent-rules-and-practic.alt: Cheat sheet of six exponent rules: product, power of a power, quotient, zero exponent, negative exponent, and fractional exponent.
sat-math-prep-exponent-rules-and-practic.figAlt: Worked example (2x³)² = 4x⁶, contrasted with the wrong answer 2x⁶ that forgets to square the coefficient.
sat-math-prep-exponent-rules-and-practic.caption: An exponent outside parentheses applies to the coefficient as well as the variable.

mastering-sat-math-questions-on-ratios-a.alt: Conversion chain turning 90 kilometers per hour into 25 meters per second by multiplying by 1000 meters per kilometer and 1 hour per 3600 seconds, with units cancelling.
mastering-sat-math-questions-on-ratios-a.figAlt: A bar split 3 to 5 representing 40 total: the 3 parts equal 15 and the 5 parts equal 25, showing that the ratio 3 to 5 has 8 parts in all.
mastering-sat-math-questions-on-ratios-a.caption: Add the ratio parts to get the whole, then divide to find the size of one part.

sat-math-practice-test-mean-median-and-d.alt: Bar chart of the data set 3, 5, 6, 8 and 28 with the median 6 and the mean 10 marked, showing the outlier 28 pulls the mean above the median.
sat-math-practice-test-mean-median-and-d.figAlt: Steps for finding a missing value: five numbers have a mean of 12 so the total is 60; four known numbers sum to 48, so the fifth number is 12.
sat-math-practice-test-mean-median-and-d.caption: Turn the mean into a total, subtract what you know, and what is left is the missing value.

sat-test-questions-right-triangle-trigon.alt: Right triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 and angle A opposite the side of length 3, giving sin A = 3/5, cos A = 4/5 and tan A = 3/4.
sat-test-questions-right-triangle-trigon.figAlt: The same 3-4-5 triangle with angles A and B, showing that the sine of one acute angle equals the cosine of the other, both 3/5.
sat-test-questions-right-triangle-trigon.caption: The two acute angles add to 90°, so the side opposite one is adjacent to the other.

sat-exam-questions-mastering-area-volume.alt: A square of side 3 and a square of side 6 showing the area grows from 9 to 36, a factor of 4, while a cube's volume grows from 27 to 216, a factor of 8.
sat-exam-questions-mastering-area-volume.figAlt: Grid of formulas: rectangle area, triangle area, circle area, rectangular prism volume, cylinder volume, and sphere volume.
sat-exam-questions-mastering-area-volume.caption: Most of these are on the SAT reference sheet, so practice reading them, not memorizing them.

sat-math-practice-exponential-functions-.alt: Graph of f(x) = 100(1.2)^x rising and g(x) = 100(0.8)^x falling, both starting at 100 when x is 0.
sat-math-practice-exponential-functions-.figAlt: The form f(x) = a times b to the x, with a as the starting value and b as the growth factor, noting that 20 percent growth means b is 1.20, not 0.20.
sat-math-practice-exponential-functions-.caption: Convert the percent to a multiplier before writing the equation.
